title: Improving Consistency Models with Generator-Induced Flows

raw.stage1:
### Purpose:
The contribution's purpose is to clarify whether the discrepancy between consistency training (CT) and consistency distillation (CD), caused by single-sample Monte Carlo estimation error, vanishes in the continuous-time limit. Paper [3] explicitly discusses the estimation error induced by single-sample Monte Carlo approximations in consistency training versus consistency distillation, but it does not address whether this discrepancy disappears in the continuous-time limit. None of the other papers establish or investigate this specific relationship. Therefore, no prior paper covers this purpose.

### Mechanism:
The contribution's mechanism involves a theoretical analysis proving that CT and CD losses converge to different pointwise values in the continuous-time limit, with a closed-form expression for the discrepancy. This includes showing that the discrepancy exists in both loss values and gradients, except in the special case of asymptotic quadratic loss. Paper [3] discusses the estimation error between CT and CD but does not provide a theoretical proof of their divergence in the continuous-time limit or derive a closed-form expression for the discrepancy. None of the other papers provide this specific theoretical analysis. Thus, the mechanism is not covered.

### Evaluation:
The evaluation facet involves a qualitative/theoretical proof (Appendix A.1) showing that the discrepancy disappears only when the difference between the velocity field and its Monte Carlo approximation vanishes, which is not satisfied under the standard independent coupling (IC) assumption. This evaluation design is unique and does not match any prior paper. While several papers (e.g., [3], [13], [17]) discuss consistency models and Monte Carlo estimators, none use this specific theoretical proof structure or address this particular claim. Therefore, the evaluation is not covered.

### Domain:
The contribution operates in the domain of generative models, specifically focusing on diffusion and consistency models for image generation. Papers [3], [7], [13], [17], [22], and [24] all work within the same general application area of generative models, diffusion models, and consistency models. While the specific problem instance (CT vs. CD discrepancy in the continuous-time limit) is new, the domain itself is well-covered by prior work.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to reduce the variance of single-sample velocity field estimation to minimize the discrepancy between consistency training (CT) and consistency diffusion (CD) when the true underlying diffusion model is inaccessible. None of the prior papers explicitly address this specific objective. While some papers (e.g., [3], [5], [11]) discuss flow matching or improving flow-based generative models, they do not target variance reduction in velocity field estimation for the stated CT/CD discrepancy. Therefore, no prior paper covers this purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism introduces "generator-induced flows," where the consistency model itself serves as a proxy for the true flow. Intermediate points are predicted from the consistency model, coupled with original noise to form "generator-induced coupling" (GC), constructing a new target flow. Papers [3], [5], [11] discuss flow matching techniques, including multisample flow matching ([5]) and consistency flow matching ([11]), which involve coupling or consistency-based methods for defining flows. Specifically, [11] enforces self-consistency in flow matching, which is conceptually similar to using the model itself as a proxy for flow. Thus, the mechanism is covered by [11].

### Evaluation
The evaluation qualitatively assesses GC's properties, such as reduced velocity field bias, lower transport cost, and improved training of consistency models (Figure 1). Papers [3], [5], [11] use similar evaluation designs for flow-based generative models, including qualitative assessments of flow properties and their impact on model training. For example, [11] evaluates flow straightness and sample quality, which aligns with the evaluation design here. Therefore, the evaluation design is covered by [11].

### Domain
The domain is generative modeling, specifically consistency models. Papers [3], [5], [11] all operate in the same general application area of generative modeling and flow-based methods. While the specific focus on consistency models may differ slightly, it falls within the broader domain of generative modeling. Thus, the domain is covered by [3], [5], and [11].

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to address the distribution shift/divergence problem in pure generator-consistency (GC) training by introducing an algorithm that enables practical training of consistency models. Paper [3] explicitly discusses mitigating sampling drift caused by imperfect score-matching in diffusion models, which is a distribution shift problem. While the specific focus differs (diffusion models vs. consistency models), the underlying objective of addressing distribution shift in generative models is substantively equivalent. Paper [19] also tackles exposure bias in diffusion models, which is another form of distribution shift during training and inference. Both papers share the same problem-class level objective of mitigating distribution shift in generative models.

### Mechanism
The contribution introduces a mixed strategy, iCT-GC(μ), which alternates between generator-consistency (GC) and standard iterative consistency (IC) with a probability μ to alleviate distribution shift caused by weak GC models on IC trajectories. Paper [3] proposes enforcing a consistency property to train on drifted data, which is conceptually similar to the mixed strategy here, as both aim to mitigate distribution shift by modifying the training process to account for drifted data. Paper [19] introduces multi-step denoising scheduled sampling to alleviate exposure bias in diffusion models, which also involves modifying the training process to address distribution shift. Both papers share the same underlying mechanism of adjusting training strategies to mitigate distribution shift in generative models.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates the proposed method using FID scores across four datasets (CIFAR-10, ImageNet32, CelebA64, LSUN Church64) and identifies μ=0.5~0.7 as the sweet spot for convergence speed and final FID. Paper [16] evaluates consistency models using FID scores, which is the same benchmark family and metric semantics. Paper [3] also uses FID scores to evaluate the effectiveness of their consistency property in mitigating sampling drift. Since FID is a standard metric for generative model evaluation, the evaluation design is covered by prior work.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of generative models for image generation. Papers [3], [16], [13], and [19] all work in the same general application area of generative models for image generation, even though they target different specific sub-problems or datasets. The domain is therefore covered.
